opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the way we think about it is that the primary reader of our documentation increasingly isn't a human at all — it's an agent. When we started Parallel, the thesis was that AI agents are going to become the dominant users of the web, more so than people. And if you take that seriously, it changes how you think about almost everything, including docs.

So when we write documentation, we're asking: if a coding agent is trying to integrate our Search API or our Task API on behalf of a developer, can it read this, understand exactly what the endpoints do, what the parameters mean, what the trade-offs are between different processors, and get it right on the first try? That means being very explicit, very structured, avoiding ambiguity that a human might gloss over with intuition but a model might misinterpret. We make sure things are available in machine-friendly formats, that examples are complete and runnable, and that the reasoning behind design choices is spelled out rather than implied.

There's still a human in the loop, of course. A developer is often deciding whether to use us, evaluating quality, cost, and latency. So the docs need to serve that person too. But what we've found is that writing for the agent first actually makes the docs better for humans as well. Clarity and precision help everyone.

And I think this is a broader pattern. Many companies are still designing their developer experience for a human sitting at a keyboard reading a web page. We think the more durable bet is to assume that the first consumer of your product interface — whether that's documentation, an API, or the web itself — is going to be an AI, and to design for that from the ground up.

r001.rationale: It says the primary reader of Parallel’s documentation increasingly is an agent, and describes coding agents integrating its APIs.

r002.rationale: It describes writing and structuring documentation for agents, but does not say Parallel tests the documentation with or for agents.

fable-5.1.text:
The honest answer is that the primary audience for our documentation isn't a person at all. It's an AI agent.

When we started Parallel, we made a pretty deliberate bet that the web was going to have a second customer. For thirty years, every piece of infrastructure on the internet was built for a human sitting in front of a browser. Search results pages, ten blue links, ads, all of it optimized for human attention. We think the next decade is about AIs being the dominant consumer of web data, and that changes how you think about everything, including something as mundane as docs.

So in practice, when we write documentation, we're asking: if Claude or a coding agent reads this, can it correctly call our API on the first try? Is the schema unambiguous? Are the examples complete enough to be copied without a human filling in gaps? Agents are very literal readers. They don't infer intent the way an experienced engineer skims a page and knows what you meant. If there's an inconsistency between the reference and a tutorial, a human shrugs and tries both. An agent gets stuck or hallucinates a parameter.

That turns out to be a wonderful forcing function, because documentation that's clear enough for a model is almost always clearer for the humans too. The developer who integrates us is usually sitting next to an agent anyway. They prompt it, it reads our docs, it writes the integration, and they review it. So the human is still in the loop, but increasingly as an editor rather than the first reader.

The other thing I'd say is that the audience shapes the product, not just the prose. We expose things like calibrated confidence and structured citations because an agent making decisions on top of our output needs to know how much to trust it. A human can look at a page and judge it. A model needs that signal in the response itself. So "who are the docs for" and "what does the API return" end up being the same question for us.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says the primary audience for Parallel’s documentation is an AI agent.

r002.rationale: It describes checking whether Claude or a coding agent can read the docs and call the API correctly on the first try, which communicates testing the documentation for agent use.

astra-6.text: I think of the primary audience as the agent that’s going to read the documentation and write code against the API. A developer might say, “Use Parallel to do this,” and then the agent has to figure out which API to call, what the inputs are, and how to interpret the outputs. So the documentation needs to be explicit, consistent, and easy to use without a lot of implicit context. Humans still need to understand it, of course, but I think it’s useful to design around that agent’s ability to successfully complete the task.

r001.rationale: It identifies the agent that will read the documentation and write code against the API as the primary audience.

r002.rationale: It discusses designing documentation for agents but does not state that Parallel tests its documentation for agent consumption.
